# Alcohol-associated hepatitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the liver > Alcohol-associated hepatitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/Ys0nth)

---

## Summary

<u>Alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u> is a clinical syndrome with a broad range of manifestations, from vague <u>malaise</u> to <u>fulminant liver failure</u>. The diagnosis should be considered in patients with a history of <u>heavy alcohol use</u> who develop <u>jaundice</u>, <u>fever</u>, <u>leukocytosis</u>, and tender <u>hepatomegaly</u>. Typical <u>liver chemistry</u> findings include <u>elevated transaminases</u> and <u>hyperbilirubinemia</u>. Diagnosis is often clinical, with <u>liver biopsy</u> reserved for uncertain cases after excluding other differential diagnoses. The <u>MELD score</u> helps assess disease severity and prognosis and guide therapy. Complete <u>alcohol</u> abstinence is the key intervention. <u>Supportive care</u> includes <u>nutritional support</u>, monitoring for <u>alcohol withdrawal</u>, and <u>treatment for alcohol use disorder</u>. Patients with <u>severe alcohol-associated hepatitis</u> may benefit from <u>glucocorticoids</u> (with or without N-acetyl <u>cysteine</u>) or early <u>liver transplantation</u>. Those unresponsive to <u>glucocorticoids</u> and ineligible for transplant should be referred for <u>palliative care</u>.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Risk factors</u> include: [[2]](/library/Rlbl9F)[[3]](/library/-nXDDA)[[4]](/library/QtcuWV0)[[5]](/library/eFcxSV0)

* History of chronic <u>heavy alcohol use</u>

* <u>Cigarette smoking</u>

* Genetic predisposition

* Female sex  [[5]](/library/eFcxSV0)

* Nutritional factors: <u>obesity</u>, <u>malnutrition</u>

* Viral <u>hepatitis</u>: e.g., <u>hepatitis C</u>

---

## Clinical features

* Acute <u>hepatitis</u>: : tender <u>hepatomegaly</u>, acute <u>jaundice</u>, <u>malaise</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>anorexia</u>, fatigue, <u>fever</u>, weight loss, <u>tachypnea</u>

* Acute <u>alcohol withdrawal</u>: <u>tremor</u>, <u>agitation</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>alcohol withdrawal seizures</u>, <u>alcohol withdrawal delirium</u>

* Long-term <u>alcohol</u> use: <u>rhinophyma</u>, <u>Dupuytren contracture</u>, <u>sarcopenia</u>, temporal muscle wasting

* <u>Cirrhosis</u>:  : <u>clinical features of liver cirrhosis</u> (e.g., <u>jaundice</u>, <u>ascites</u>, <u>palmar erythema</u>, <u>spider angiomata</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Acute <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u> may be reversible in mild cases. [[2]](/library/Rlbl9F)[[3]](/library/-nXDDA)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Symptoms of alcohol-associated hepatitis</u> are nonspecific. The presence of acute-onset <u>jaundice</u> can help differentiate acute <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u> from <u>decompensated cirrhosis</u>. [[6]](/library/TFc6hV0)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[3]](/library/-nXDDA)[[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




Suspect <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u> in patients with suggestive clinical features and a history of chronic <u>heavy alcohol use</u>.




* Use the <u>consensus definitions for alcohol-associated hepatitis</u> to establish a definite, probable, or possible diagnosis.

* Obtain laboratory and imaging studies to support the diagnosis and rule out differential diagnoses.

* Perform a thorough infectious disease workup guided by clinical suspicion.

* Consider referral for transjugular <u>liver biopsy</u> if the diagnosis remains uncertain.

* Assess severity using the <u>MELD score</u> (preferred over the <u>Maddrey discriminant function</u>). [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)

* Identify patients with <u>alcohol use disorder</u> (e.g., using the <u>AUDIT-C</u> score).





> [!WARNING]
> The presence of <u>systemic inflammatory response syndrome</u> (<u>SIRS</u>) criteria at admission is a predictor of <u>multiorgan failure</u> (especially <u>AKI</u>) and early <u>death</u>. [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




> [!TIP]
> Infections are common in patients with <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u> and are associated with a poorer prognosis. An infectious disease workup is recommended in all patients. [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




### Consensus definitions for alcohol-associated hepatitis [[3]](/library/-nXDDA)[[4]](/library/QtcuWV0)[[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




* Clinical <u>diagnosis of alcohol-associated hepatitis</u>

* Onset of <u>jaundice</u> within the past 8 weeks

* ≥ 6 months of ongoing <u>alcohol</u> consumption above the threshold and < 60 continuous days of abstinence from <u>alcohol</u> before <u>jaundice</u> onset

* > 40 g <u>alcohol</u> per day for female patients

* > 60 g <u>alcohol</u> per day for male patients

* Characteristic <u>liver chemistries in alcohol-associated hepatitis</u>

* <u>Confounding</u> factors

* Atypical laboratory results

* Uncertain <u>alcohol</u> use

* Presence of other potential causes of <u>liver</u> disease; see “<u>Differential diagnoses of alcohol-associated hepatitis</u>.”

* Classification

* Definite <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u>: <u>clinical diagnosis</u> PLUS histological confirmation

* Probable <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u>: <u>clinical diagnosis</u>

* Possible <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u>: uncertain <u>clinical diagnosis</u> because of the presence of <u>confounding</u> factors





### Initial studies [[3]](/library/-nXDDA)[[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




* Liver chemistries in alcohol-associated hepatitis

* <u>AST</u>: > 50 IU/L

* Both <u>AST</u> and <u>ALT</u>: < 400 IU/L

* <u>AST:ALT ratio</u>: > 1.5

* Total <u>bilirubin</u>: > 3 mg/dL

* Additional <u>liver studies</u> [[4]](/library/QtcuWV0)

* <u>GGT</u>: > 100 IU/L

* <u>ALP</u>: ↑

* <u>INR</u>: > 1.5

* <u>Albumin</u>: < 3 g/dL

* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>WBC</u>: > 12,000/mmÂ³

* <u>Platelets</u>: ↓ or ↑

* <u>Macrocytic anemia</u>;  (↓ <u>hemoglobin</u> with ↑ <u>MCV</u>)

* <u>BMP</u>: to assess for <u>AKI</u> and calculate severity scores





> [!NOTE]
> <u>AST</u> > <u>ALT</u> in <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u>: Remember “make a toAST with <u>alcohol</u>!”




#### Imaging studies [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




Obtain imaging studies in all patients to rule out differential diagnoses (e.g., <u>portal vein thrombosis</u>, <u>Budd-Chiari syndrome</u>, <u>HCC</u>, <u>biliary obstruction</u> with <u>cholangitis</u>).  [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




* <u>RUQ</u> <u>ultrasound</u> with Doppler:  (preferred): may show findings of <u>fatty liver</u> disease;  (e.g., <u>steatosis</u>, <u>hepatomegaly</u>, and periportal <u>edema</u>) and/or <u>cirrhosis</u> [[5]](/library/eFcxSV0)

* CT or <u>MRI</u> abdomen: : may show findings of <u>fatty liver</u> disease ; (e.g., decreased <u>liver</u> attenuation, heterogeneous <u>steatosis</u>) and/or <u>cirrhosis</u> [[5]](/library/eFcxSV0)[[8]](/library/UFcbhV0)





### Additional diagnostic workup [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[9]](/library/JLXsAA)




Obtain additional studies to exclude differential diagnoses and identify comorbidities; workup should be guided by clinical suspicion and may include the following:




* Infection

* <u>Workup for sepsis</u>

* <u>Viral hepatitis panel</u>

* <u>Autoimmune hepatitis</u>: e.g., <u>ANAs</u>, <u>anti-smooth muscle antibodies</u>, <u>IgG</u> levels

* <u>Metabolic liver disease</u>: e.g., serum <u>ceruloplasmin</u>, <u>alpha-1 antitrypsin</u> levels

* <u>Drug-induced liver injury</u>: e.g., <u>medication review</u>, urine toxicology, <u>serum acetaminophen levels</u>

* <u>Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease</u> (<u>MASLD</u>): e.g., <u>alcohol-associated liver disease</u>/<u>nonalcoholic fatty liver disease</u> index (ANI) to help differentiate <u>alcohol-associated liver disease</u> from <u>MASLD</u> [[10]](/library/y-cd-U0)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Sepsis</u> should always be ruled out in patients with <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u> and <u>SIRS</u>.




### <u>Liver biopsy</u> [[3]](/library/-nXDDA)[[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




* Indications:  (not routinely recommended)

* Unclear diagnosis because of the presence of <u>confounding</u> factors (e.g., chronic <u>jaundice</u>)

* Uncertain <u>alcohol</u> consumption

* Recruitment to a clinical trial

* Technique: Transjugular <u>liver biopsy</u> is preferred. [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)

* Findings: signs of alcoholic <u>steatohepatitis</u> and/or <u>cirrhosis</u> (see “Pathology” in “<u>Alcoholic liver disease</u>” for details).





> [!TIP]
> Histopathological findings of <u>alcohol-associated steatohepatitis</u> may be indistinguishable from findings of <u>metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis</u>; the ANI can help differentiate between the two.

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[3]](/library/-nXDDA)[[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




* Advise immediate <u>alcohol</u> cessation; no amount of <u>alcohol</u> consumption is considered safe. [[6]](/library/TFc6hV0)

* Assess for <u>alcohol withdrawal syndrome</u>: Calculate the patient's <u>CIWA-Ar</u> score.  [[6]](/library/TFc6hV0)[[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)

* Provide <u>management for alcohol withdrawal</u> (e.g., <u>benzodiazepines</u>), and <u>management of alcohol use disorder</u>.

* Ensure adequate calorie and <u>micronutrient</u> intake.

* In patients with severe disease (i.e., <u>MELD</u> > 20), consider <u>glucocorticoid</u> therapy, IV <u>n-acetylcysteine</u> (<u>NAC</u>), and referral for early <u>liver transplantation</u>.

* Prevent and manage comorbidities and complications.

* Consult <u>palliative care</u> for patients who do not improve with <u>glucocorticoid</u> therapy and are not eligible for early <u>liver transplant</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Alcohol</u> cessation is the only management strategy with proven long-term benefits in <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u>. [[3]](/library/-nXDDA)[[5]](/library/eFcxSV0)[[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Alcohol</u> cessation may lead to <u>alcohol withdrawal syndrome</u>. [[2]](/library/Rlbl9F)




![Clinical institute withdrawal assessment for alcohol (CIWA-Ar)](media/a2flp2npdwufpspqckjlslv4.jpg)

Clinical institute withdrawal assessment for alcohol (CIWA-Ar)




### Disposition [[2]](/library/Rlbl9F)




Consider <u>ICU</u> admission in any of the following situations:




* Extrahepatic organ failure

* Stage III or IV <u>hepatic encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Respiratory failure</u> or the need for ventilatory support

* <u>Hemodynamic instability</u> or <u>septic shock</u>





### <u>Nutritional support</u> [[3]](/library/-nXDDA)[[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[15]](/library/hydcUs0)




Severe <u>malnutrition</u> is common in patients with <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u>.




* Routinely perform a <u>malnutrition assessment in adults</u>.

* Consider consultation for <u>specialized nutritional support</u>.

* <u>Enteral nutrition</u> is preferred.

* Recommended daily caloric intake: 35–40 kcal/kg

* Recommended daily protein requirement: 1.2–1.5 g/kg

* Assess for and treat <u>micronutrient</u> deficiencies, e.g.:

* <u>Zinc deficiency</u> and deficiency of other <u>trace elements</u>

* <u>Thiamine deficiency</u> and deficiency of other <u>B-complex vitamins</u>

* <u>Volume replacement</u>: IV <u>albumin</u> is preferred over IV <u>crystalloids</u>.





### Pharmacological therapy [[3]](/library/-nXDDA)[[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




#### <u>Glucocorticoids</u>  [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




* Indication: : <u>Severe alcohol-associated hepatitis</u> (i.e., <u>MELD score</u> > 20)  and no contraindications  [[3]](/library/-nXDDA)[[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)

* Preferred agents

* <u>Prednisolone</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)

* <u>Methylprednisolone</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE  [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)

* Monitoring: Calculate the <u>Lille score</u> to assess response after 4 or 7 days of treatment with <u>glucocorticoids</u>. [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[12]](/library/ftck1V0)

* <u>Lille score</u> > 0.45: Patient is not responding; stop <u>glucocorticoids</u> and consider further treatment options (e.g., <u>supportive care</u>, <u>palliative care</u>, early <u>liver transplantation</u>).

* <u>Lille score</u> ≤ 0.45: Patient is responding; continue <u>glucocorticoids</u> to complete 28 days of treatment, followed by 2–4 weeks of taper.





> [!TIP]
> Patients who do not respond within the first week of <u>glucocorticoid</u> treatment are unlikely to derive benefit from continued treatment. [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)




#### Other medications [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[16]](/library/3FcS3V0)




* N-<u>Acetylcysteine</u> [[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[17]](/library/FycgSU0)

* May reduce complications and mortality when given as a 5-day infusion in combination with <u>glucocorticoids</u>

* Evidence that <u>N-acetylcysteine</u> improves outcomes is limited, but the risks of treatment are low.

* <u>Pentoxifylline</u>: no longer recommended





### Early <u>liver transplantation</u> [[3]](/library/-nXDDA)[[7]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[18]](/library/LZ1wX20)




* Definition: <u>liver transplantation</u> without 6 months of abstinence from <u>alcohol</u>

* Consider in patients with the following:

* No response to medical management

* Favorable psychosocial profiles





> [!TIP]
> <u>Liver transplantation</u> should be considered in selected patients with acute <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>hepatitis</u>, even if they have not abstained from <u>alcohol</u> for the required 6 months.




### Management of complications and comorbidities




Monitor for and manage the following:




* Infection and <u>sepsis</u> (routine use of prophylactic <u>antibiotics</u> is not recommended)

* <u>Complications of cirrhosis</u> (e.g., <u>ascites</u>, <u>hepatic encephalopathy</u>, <u>esophageal variceal hemorrhage</u>)

* <u>Prevention of AKI</u> and <u>hepatorenal syndrome</u> (e.g., avoidance of <u>nephrotoxins</u> and cautious use of <u>diuretics</u>)

* Mental health disorders and psychosocial factors (e.g., <u>major depressive disorder</u>, <u>generalized anxiety disorder</u>)
